transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-30
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Recording: enabled
Notes: SE-led deep dive on sealed image transfer, offline license activation, GPU driver compat, KV pre-warm and perf targets.

Summary:
Voyager needs an air-gapped install path for Redwood Private: signed bundle transfer via removable media, offline license activation (permanent entitlements per cluster), and kernel/driver tuning for their 8xA100 nodes. Primary success criteria are: reproducible 95th pct latency under 120ms for typical 512-token generations, and sustained throughput of ~60 reqs/min at 2k context for peak load. Security needs attestations and manifest checksums.

Topics covered:
- Sealed bundle format and manifest signing
- Transport options (sneakernet, S3 presigned + gateway, partner transfer appliance)
- Offline license activation flow and entitlement signing
- GPU driver/kernel module versions and validation steps
- KV cache warmup strategies and continuous batching config
- Quantization compatibility and fallbacks for lower memory nodes
- Benchmark plan and measurement artifacts

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alicia Park (Redwood AE): cool, alright everyone thanks for joining, um let's do quick intros and then Marco will run through the sealed bundle flow.
[00:07] Priya Menon (Voyager): hi, Priya here, head of m-l-ops, I'll be owning the pilot and sign-off.
[00:10] Evan Zhou (Voyager): Evan, infra eng, I'll be doing the on-prem install and driver work.
[00:13] Marco Diaz (Redwood SE): Marco here, runtime lead, I'll dig into kv, batching, and kernel bits.
[00:16] Lydia Park (Voyager Security): Lydia, security. interested in attestations and audit traces.
[00:19] Alicia Park: great, Marco, over to you.

[02:03] Marco Diaz: ok, so first off the sealed bundle: we ship a tar.gz that's GPG-signed, inside you get: model shards, runtime artifact (redwood-runner binary), the kernel helper modules if needed, a manifest.json with sha256 checksums and a signing cert chain. we also produce an offline license file (.lic) that's encrypted and bound to the cluster id.
[02:29] Evan Zhou: when you say bound to cluster id, can you explain the binding? we don't want a phone-home requirement.
[02:36] Marco Diaz: yes, absolutely. the offline activation works by you generating a cluster attestation (a hardware fingerprint) — we accept an HSM-signed CSR or a signed manifest from your HSM/TPM. you send that CSR to Redwood by a secure channel (or via a partner courier on a usb drive) and we return a signed entitlement blob. there's no runtime phone-home; the entitlement is asymmetric-signed and the runner verifies the signature locally.
[03:10] Lydia Park: so the verification uses the cert chain you included in the sealed bundle? where is the root kept?
[03:17] Marco Diaz: the root CA is Redwood's offline root; the runner ships with the root cert pinned. the entitlement contains a validity window as well as the cluster fingerprint. all verification happens local to the node. you'll get an audit log entry we can include in the manifest showing the entitlement issuance.

[05:42] Evan Zhou: ok, switching to driver stuff — our infra team is on a custom RHEL 8 kernel, with vendor-patched drivers. we need to know exactly which nvidia kernel module versions and kernel config options you validated.
[05:55] Marco Diaz: got it. we'll provide a driver compatibility matrix. quick note: for A100s we recommend driver 525.x or newer with the nvidia-modprobe helper and the patched NVLINK firmware from the vendor. additionally, RTX kernel modules are optional but we include our shim module redwood_kmod which decides whether to use cuda or a fallback path. for air-gapped installs we include the kmod and insmod scripts.
[06:30] Priya Menon: does the shim require any special kernel flags? we have kexec disabled in prod.
[06:36] Marco Diaz: no kexec required; the shim uses standard module registration. on RHEL we usually enable CONFIG_KALLSYMS for symbol lookup and CONFIG_NET so the loader can bind to udev events; we'll send a list of minimal kernel config flags.

[09:12] Marco Diaz: next, kv cache warmup — this is a big one for preserving latency. if you start cold, the first few requests will be expensive because KV pages populate. we recommend a two-stage approach: prefix-warmup from a representative prompt corpus, then a continuous background prefetcher that keeps recent keys resident. the sealed bundle includes a warmup harness script you can run during staging.
[09:40] Evan Zhou: realistic question — how long does warmup take for a 13B-ish model with 32k kv entries? our node memory is limited.
[09:48] Marco Diaz: for 13B with 32k entries on A100 40GB, expect ~8-12 minutes to get to steady-state if you run the provided corpus at a 10qps pace. with an 8xA100 cluster in parallel you can shorten wall-clock warmup if you shard the corpus across nodes. the KV prefetcher supports eviction policies; we default to LRU with pinned prefixes.

[12:05] Tom Ward (Voyager): during the warmup whats the token throughput and do we hit GPU memory spikes? we had OOMs on prior model loads.
[12:12] Marco Diaz: you will see short-lived memory spikes while populating KV, mostly driven by batch-size times sequence length. to avoid OOMs we suggest running with quantized kernels if you need lower memory. our quantized kernels (8-bit or 4-bit profiles) reduce memory overhead by ~35-60% depending on config. we've included fallback quant profiles in the sealed bundle; runner auto-selects based on available CUDA memory.

[15:00] Priya Menon: tell me more about quantization safety — we have clinical text workloads and need deterministic outputs or at least bounded drift.
[15:09] Marco Diaz: yes, quantization introduces small distribution shifts. we provide a quality regression harness and delta-checks. recommended practice: run the baseline eval set with fp16+optimizer then with each quant profile; we track token-level edit distance and semantic similarity. for high-sensitivity flows we keep a canary route pinned to fp16 for critical cases.

[18:44] Marco Diaz: batching and continuous batching: we support adaptive batching windows to balance latency/throughput. for your target 2k context and 60 reqs/min, we recommend a batch_target of 4-8 and an adaptive window of 15-30ms to avoid 95th percentile spikes. the runner also supports per-route SLOs so you can prioritize low-latency routes with smaller batch caps.

[22:12] Lydia Park: audit logs — we need cryptographically verifiable install logs and activation events. is that possible?
[22:20] Marco Diaz: yes, the offline bundle includes an audit collector that signs install steps with the node's TPM key and produces a signed install artifact (JSONL) you can keep. the entitlement issuance step includes a signed issuance token from Redwood; we add that to the manifest. that should satisfy SOC-type audit requests.

[26:30] Evan Zhou: question about transfer integrity — if we ship via AWS Snowball or via courier USB, what's the recommended checksum process?
[26:38] Marco Diaz: we sign the manifest and include sha256 checksums for each artifact. during import you run the verify script that checks signature chain and each sha256. for physical media we also recommend a tamper-evident seal and a video chain-of-custody; we can provide a template chain-of-custody doc.

[30:55] Marco Diaz: now benchmarks — we ran internal tests on 8xA100 80GB with a 13B-like model and saw steady-state throughput of ~70 reqs/min at 2k context with 6 batching target and adaptive window 20ms; 95th latency for 512-token generation was ~98ms. those numbers depend on your kernel flags, driver version and whether KV is warmed. cold starts were closer to 450-600ms.
[31:21] Priya Menon: ok, acceptable. can we reproduce those numbers on our 8x40GB cluster?
[31:26] Marco Diaz: yes, we expect ~10-20% delta due to memory. we'll provide the perf harness (a script + dataset) in the sealed bundle; the plan is you run the harness during a 4-hour window and send the results back. we'll compare metrics and tune batch settings.

[35:10] Evan Zhou: are there any kernel patches that we must apply? our vendor backports a lot.
[35:16] Marco Diaz: typically no kernel source patching; the critical pieces are driver version and firmware. if vendor backports are compatible we just need the pinning for module ABI. if not, we provide a prebuilt module that matches the kernel ABI; that's why we include the redwood_kmod. if your vendor forbids unsigned modules, we can provide signed modules tied to your kernel key or work with your vendor to sign.

[38:50] Tom Ward: for the offline license file, is there a way to revoke or rotate entitlements?
[38:57] Marco Diaz: yes, entitlements are revocable. we issue revocation lists as part of periodic manifests; you can also present a revoked list to the runner. for emergency revocation we can issue a short-lived revocation manifest you import manually.

[41:05] Alicia Park: quick commercial note — pricing for offline licensing includes a platform fee plus per-node entitlements; Alicia to follow up with the exact numbers.

[43:12] Marco Diaz: summarizing recommended next steps for the pilot: 1) Redwood to produce signed sealed bundle + manifest + perf harness 2) Voyager to pick a 4-hour perf window and provide cluster fingerprint (TPM CSR) 3) transfer sealed bundle via chosen transport 4) run warmup + perf harness and return results.

[44:02] Priya Menon: sounds good. question — are there limits on concurrency for the entitlement? if we have burst capacity with dedicated nodes?
[44:10] Marco Diaz: entitlements are per-cluster but you can include a licensing attribute for reserved capacity and burst allowances. we'll include that in the license addendum.

[47:33] Lydia Park: on attestation docs, can Redwood provide template text for our security review? like how the root CA is handled, signing process, and audit log formats.
[47:41] Marco Diaz: yes, we'll provide an attestation pack — a short PDF describing cert chain, verification steps, sample signed install log, and the manifest structure.

[49:55] Priya Menon: ok, last question — what does rollback look like if a bundle fails at import?
[50:02] Marco Diaz: import is transactional: the verify script checks signatures and checksums first, then does a staged install in /opt/redwood/tmp and only switches symlinks after a final verification. if something fails you'll roll back to the previous runner binary. we'll make sure to document the exact commands.

[51:22] Alicia Park: great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the bundle link and docs. Marco, can you own the driver matrix and warmup guidance?
[51:29] Marco Diaz: yeah I'll own that.
[51:32] Priya Menon: thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.
